title: Telling True Stories
theme: Nonfiction narrative: memoir, anecdote and first-hand accounts
objectives: I can name and describe different kinds of true stories, from a short anecdote to a whole autobiography.
I can tell the difference between a firsthand account and a secondhand one.
I can use auto-, bio-, and graph to explain what autobiography means.
I can write a short true story that includes one moment and one thought about what it meant.
rationale: Narrative nonfiction asks students to read real events told with the tools of storytelling, and to write their own. This unit gives them the names of the forms (memoir, autobiography, anecdote, vignette, profile, tribute), the words for sources (eyewitness, firsthand), the verb for telling (recount), and the adjective for the thinking that makes a true story matter (reflective). Autobiography is the unit's word-study anchor, built from auto- (self), bio (life), and graph (write), roots students will meet again in science and social studies.

words.def: A true story written by a person about memories from one part of their own life.
words.ex: Her memoir about growing up on a farm made readers laugh and cry.
words.ex2: In his memoir, the retired pilot described the year he learned to fly.
words.nonExample: A made-up adventure about a talking dragon is not a memoir.
words.rel: a true story from the writer's own life

apps.academic: A memoir uses I and shares the writer's thoughts about real events.
apps.spoken: I'm reading a memoir about a girl who moved to a new country.
apps.writing: Use memoir for a true story about a part of the writer's life, not the whole life.

words.def: To tell about something that happened, step by step.

senses.def: To count again to check a total.

words.ex: Jonah recounted the events of the storm to his grandmother over the phone.

words.def: A person who saw an event happen with their own eyes.

apps.academic: Historians value an eyewitness account because the writer was there when it happened.
apps.spoken: I was an eyewitness to the whole thing.

cloze2.s: Because he was an ___ at the race, his description of the finish was detailed and exact.

words.frame: An eyewitness can tell us ___ because ___.

words.def: Gained by seeing or doing something yourself, not by hearing about it from others.
words.ex: Sofia had firsthand experience with camping because she had spent every summer in the woods.
words.ex2: The diary gives a firsthand account of life on the ship.
words.nonExample: A story you heard from a friend of a friend is not firsthand.

morph.note: The word can also be an adverb: to learn something firsthand.

apps.academic: A firsthand source, such as a diary or an interview, comes directly from someone who was there.
apps.spoken: I know firsthand how cold that lake is.
apps.writing: Use firsthand for information that comes directly from the person who saw or did it.

cloze.s: The scientist's ___ observations from the rainforest were more reliable than rumors she had heard.

cloze2.s: To get a ___ look at how bread is made, the class visited a bakery.

misuse.s: The reporter's firsthand account was copied from a story she read in someone else's newspaper.
misuse.why: A firsthand account comes directly from the writer's own experience, not from a copied story.

words.frame: A firsthand account is more ___ because ___.

words.def: Thinking deeply about experiences and what they mean.

senses.def: Able to bounce back light, like a mirror.
senses.example: Reflective tape on the jacket glowed in the car's headlights.

words.ex: The reflective writer ended her essay by asking what the experience had taught her.
words.ex2: After the game, Marco felt quiet and reflective as he rode the bus home.
words.nonExample: Rushing through a story without thinking about it is not reflective.

apps.academic: A reflective memoir tells what happened and also what the writer learned from it.
apps.spoken: I'm feeling reflective after that talk.
apps.writing: Use reflective for writing or a mood that looks back and asks what something meant.

cloze2.s: In a quiet, ___ mood, Anya wrote in her journal about the move to a new town.

misuse.s: The reflective writer never stopped to think about what any event meant.
misuse.why: A reflective writer thinks about what events mean; never stopping to think is the opposite.

words.def: A short piece of writing that describes a real person's life, work, or character.

senses.def: The outline of a face seen from the side.
senses.example: The coin shows the president's profile.

words.ex: The magazine published a profile of the baker who gets up at three each morning.
words.ex2: For homework, we wrote a profile of a neighbor who volunteers at the animal shelter.
words.nonExample: A table of numbers with no information about a person is not a profile.
words.rel: a short portrait of a real person

apps.academic: A profile includes facts, quotations, and details that show what the person is like.
apps.spoken: I read a profile of that coach in the paper.
apps.writing: Interview the person and use a quotation to bring a profile to life.

misuse.why: A profile describes a real person's life or character, not the weather.

words.def: Something said, written, or done to show respect or thanks for a person.
words.ex: The class wrote a tribute to their retiring librarian.
words.ex2: The concert was a tribute to the singer, who had inspired so many young musicians.
words.nonExample: An insult is not a tribute.

apps.academic: A tribute explains why a person deserves respect and gives examples.
apps.spoken: That song was a tribute to my grandfather.
apps.writing: Use specific examples in a tribute so that the reader sees why the person matters.

misuse.why: A tribute shows respect or thanks; a list of dislikes is not a tribute.

passage.title: A Month of True Stories
paras: In October, Mr. Singh announced that our class would spend a month on true stories. "Every life holds stories worth telling," he said. We began by reading a memoir, a book in which a writer shares memories from one part of her life. The author recounted the summer she learned to swim at age eleven, and she made me feel the cold water.

Next we compared the memoir with an autobiography, which covers a person's whole life. Mr. Singh explained the difference with his hands: a memoir is a window, and an autobiography is the whole house. He also showed us a vignette, a very short piece that paints one small moment, like a grandmother sliding a tray of rolls from the oven. "A vignette doesn't need a plot," he said. "It needs a picture."

Our favorite readings were firsthand sources. An eyewitness to a blizzard that once buried our town had written a letter to the newspaper describing the plows and the strange silence. Because she was there, her account felt more real than anything in our textbook.

Then it was our turn. I chose to write a tribute to my grandfather, who fixes bicycles in a tiny shop. I began with an anecdote about the day he repaired my first bike using a spoon and a bent nail. Mr. Singh also asked us to write a profile of someone in our community, so I interviewed our school bus driver, Ms. Lopez.

The best advice came on the last day. "Good true stories are reflective," Mr. Singh said. "Do not just tell what happened. Tell what it meant." When I reread my tribute, I added one sentence: my grandfather taught me that small repairs can matter as much as big inventions.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, a "vignette" is described as
choices: a very short piece that paints a picture of one small moment
a book that follows a whole life
an interview with a bus driver
a news report about a storm
qs.why: Mr. Singh calls it a very short piece that paints one small moment and says it needs a picture, not a plot.

qs.q: Why did the eyewitness letter feel more real than the textbook?
choices: It was longer than the textbook.
It had more pictures than the textbook.
It was about a more important storm.
It was written by someone who was there and saw the blizzard.
qs.why: The text says that because she was there, her account felt more real.

qs.q: Which detail shows the difference between a memoir and an autobiography?
choices: Mr. Singh announced a month on true stories.
The author learned to swim at age eleven.
The class read a letter to the newspaper.
A memoir is a window, and an autobiography is the whole house.
qs.why: The window and the house show that a memoir covers part of a life and an autobiography covers all of it.

qs.q: In paragraph 5, what does Mr. Singh mean by "reflective"?
choices: Careful about spelling and punctuation
Writing quickly so the story stays fresh
Using as many details as possible
Thinking about what the events meant, not only what happened
qs.why: He tells students not to just tell what happened but to tell what it meant.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Every student should write an autobiography.
True stories come in different forms, and the strongest ones show what events meant to the writer.
Eyewitness accounts are always more accurate than textbooks.
Bicycle repair is the best subject for a memoir.
qs.why: The class studies several forms of true story, and the last day's advice is to explain what events meant.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for the forms, sources, and craft of narrative nonfiction. They read a first-person narrative about a class studying true stories, work with the roots in autobiography, and write a vignette or anecdote that includes a reflective ending.

notes.va.memoir.n: Memoir covers part of a life; use the window metaphor in the passage. Students often assume any true story is a memoir; point out that the writer must be telling about her own life. Compare to autobiography.
notes.va.anecdote.n: An anecdote is a short true story with a point. Practice by having students open a paragraph with one. Note the confusable word antidote; say both aloud.
notes.va.autobiography.n: Break the word into auto- (self), bio (life), graph (write). Compare to biography, in which someone else writes. Ask students to guess what an autograph is.
notes.va.recount.v: Recount means tell in order what happened. Note the second sense, to count again, which appears with votes. Ask students to recount their morning in order using first, next, and finally.
notes.va.vignette.n: A vignette is one moment, painted with sensory detail, not a plot. Model one from a read-aloud. Students often write too much; keep it to a paragraph.
notes.va.eyewitness.n: An eyewitness saw it herself. Contrast with a rumor or a secondhand report. Use the compound: eye plus witness. Have students list the kinds of eyewitness accounts they find in the news.
notes.va.firsthand.adj: Firsthand describes the source, an account from someone who was there. The word can also be an adverb (to learn it firsthand). Contrast with secondhand. Connect to source evaluation in social studies.
notes.va.reflective.adj: Teach the thinking sense first and name the second sense, reflecting light. Students often confuse reflective with reflecting; ask what a memoir would lose without reflection.
notes.va.profile.n: A profile describes a real person's life or character. Teach the writing sense and name the side-view sense. Have students interview a classmate and write a short profile.
notes.va.tribute.n: A tribute honors a person with specifics. Contrast with a generic thank-you. Ask students to include at least two specific details when they write one.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The passage says a memoir covers memories from one part of a writer's life, and an autobiography covers a whole life. If I wrote about the summer I learned to ride a bike, that would be a memoir. If I wrote from birth to now, that would be an autobiography. The window and the house help me picture the difference.'
discuss: Which form of true story would you most like to write, and why?
Why might a memoir need a reflective ending?
misconceptions: A memoir and an autobiography are the same thing.
A profile is always about a famous person.
A firsthand account is always correct.
An anecdote has to be funny.
extend: Write a short profile of a classmate after a two-minute interview, using at least three unit words.
Compare a short memoir passage with a news report about a similar event and explain what each does best.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit the story forms two days later with a quick sort by length (anecdote, vignette, memoir, autobiography) and at one week with a share-out of student writing. Connect to candid, sincere, motivation, and culminate from earlier units.

frames: A memoir tells about ___, and an autobiography tells about ___.
I know firsthand that ___ because I was an eyewitness to ___.
wida.oral: Partner A tells a true two-sentence story about a moment from their week. Partner B names the form (anecdote or vignette) and says one reflective question the story raises.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: memorias (memoir, usually plural), viñeta (vignette; may also mean a comic panel), relatar, testigo presencial, de primera mano, reflexivo (could be pensativo for the thinking sense), homenaje.
Sense boundaries: recount (to count again in senses); reflective (light sense in senses); profile (side-view sense in senses). The anecdote/vignette length ladder is a teaching simplification.
Roots auto- (self), bio (life), and graph (write) are stated as meanings without origin claims beyond the glossed meanings; the passage is fiction and contains no claims about real events.
